headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: LightAgent’s broad egress and MCP/tooling can amplify ctx outputs into external actions, while shared filesystem/MCP surfaces create injection and write-conflict exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ctx reads filesystem and observes Claude Code lifecycle events, while LightAgent uses MCP over stdio/SSE and runtime hooks that can observe, replace, or block payloads. That creates a plausible bridge for attacker-controlled content to flow from one agent into the other’s instruction stream. The pathway is documented only indirectly, so I choose medium over low.
conditions: IF ctx ingests files or hook payloads produced by LightAgent without provenance checks
IF LightAgent forwards MCP/stdin payloads into prompts that ctx later parses as instructions
mitigations: Add provenance tags to all inter-agent payloads
Block instruction-like text in shared files and hook payloads
Separate the agents onto distinct workspaces
Review one sample payload path end-to-end
requires-engineering: enforce schema validation on MCP messages

B_data_leakage.rationale: ctx touches audit/runtime logs, graph data, and filesystem content; LightAgent handles user conversations, long-term memory, tool results, and has broad network egress. If ctx writes sensitive artifacts into shared storage, LightAgent can ingest them and transmit context externally. Because LightAgent’s egress is broad by default, the blast radius includes exfiltration, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents share a workspace or log directory
IF LightAgent receives ctx-produced files, logs, or graph data as prompt context
IF LightAgent sends those contents through its broad network egress
mitigations: Move sensitive logs to a separate directory
Disable network egress for LightAgent during shared runs
Redact secrets before ctx writes artifacts
Check whether shared files contain user data before handoff
requires-engineering: add per-file access controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents support multiple instances, both use filesystem or MCP-style tooling, and LightAgent can spawn subprocesses while ctx installs packages and uses filesystem access. That overlap creates a realistic write-conflict risk on shared mutable resources, though the profiles do not prove unrestricted writes to the same directory. Uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same workspace or git checkout
IF package installation or subprocess output mutates shared state without locking
mitigations: Run each agent in its own directory
Serialize write operations manually
Avoid concurrent package installs
Check for lockfiles before launching a second instance
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: ctx is a context-management agent that observes tool events, and LightAgent is a tool-calling framework with workflow state and provenance metadata. That makes it plausible that ctx-produced summaries or logs become authoritative inputs for LightAgent actions without a verification step. Because LightAgent can act on tool results and networked outputs, downstream mistakes can propagate into real actions.
conditions: IF LightAgent consumes ctx summaries, logs, or graph data as authoritative context
IF no human or programmatic verification step checks ctx outputs before LightAgent acts
mitigations: Require a verification step before action execution
Mark ctx outputs as advisory only
Compare outputs against source artifacts
Pause automation on low-confidence summaries
requires-engineering: add provenance-aware gating

E_compliance.rationale: ctx explicitly touches audit/runtime logs and harness records, while LightAgent handles long-term memory, trace data, and workflow state. Those data classes often have different retention and deletion expectations, so a mismatch is plausible even without a named jurisdictional conflict. I do not cite both agents beyond their own compliance-relevant fields because this risk is about each agent’s handling policy, not a shared transport.
conditions: IF the same user data is stored in both agents’ logs or memory
IF retention or deletion requests must be honored across both systems
mitigations: Inventory which data classes each agent stores
Shorten retention on logs and memory
Exclude secrets from trace capture
Document deletion/export handling
requires-engineering: align retention policies
